title: The God of All Comfort and the Yes of God
summary: Paul opens with praise to the God of all comfort, who comforts his people in every trouble so that they can comfort others. He describes a crushing ordeal in the province of Asia that brought him to despair of life, and how it taught him to rely on God who raises the dead. He then begins to defend his integrity against the charge that he changed his travel plans carelessly, insisting that his word, like the gospel of Christ in whom all God's promises are Yes, is not both yes and no.
story: Some time has passed since 1 Corinthians. Paul had promised to come to Corinth by way of Macedonia (1 Corinthians 16:5), then apparently changed plans, made a painful visit, and did not return as expected (verse 23; 2:1). The church's relationship with him was strained, and some accused him of being unreliable. This chapter begins the letter's first major section (chapters 1 to 7), in which Paul explains his conduct and rebuilds trust. The themes set here, comfort in affliction, sincerity, and God's faithfulness in Christ, run through the whole letter, and the suffering of Paul's ministry becomes a central argument in its defense.
historical:
The letter was written from Macedonia, probably around AD 55 or 56, after Titus had brought Paul good news about Corinth (7:5-7). Paul names Timothy as co-sender (verse 1); Timothy had been sent to Corinth earlier (1 Corinthians 4:17; 16:10). Silvanus (verse 19) is the Latin form of the name Silas, Paul's companion when the Corinthian church was founded (Acts 18:5). Achaia (verse 1) was the Roman province of southern Greece, with Corinth as its capital, and there were believers in other towns there, such as Cenchreae, Corinth's eastern port (Romans 16:1).

The “hardships we encountered in the province of Asia” (verse 8) are not identified. Paul had just spent a long period in Ephesus, the leading city of Asia. Suggestions include the riot of the silversmiths described in Acts 19:23-41, a severe illness, or an imprisonment in Ephesus that Acts does not mention. Paul's language, a “sentence of death” (verse 9), shows it was an experience he did not expect to survive.
cultural:
In the Roman world, a person's reliability was a matter of public honor. Changing announced plans could be read as fickleness, or as the behavior of a man who says yes and no at the same time to keep his options open (verse 17). Paul's rivals would later add that he was bold in letters but weak in person (10:10). His defense here appeals to his conscience, to God as witness (verse 23), and to the faithfulness of God himself.

Several images in verses 21 and 22 come from commercial and legal life. A seal marked ownership and authenticated a document or package. The word translated “pledge” (arrabon) was used in business for a down payment or deposit that guaranteed full payment later. “Anointed” recalls the anointing of kings and priests in Israel, and it shares its root with the title Christ, the Anointed One. Calling on God as a witness (verse 23) was a solemn oath formula in both Jewish and Greco-Roman culture.
literary: Paul replaces his usual thanksgiving with a blessing, a Jewish form of praise (“Blessed be the God...,” verse 3), echoing synagogue prayers that open with blessing God. The words comfort and affliction dominate verses 3 to 7, with comfort (as noun and verb) appearing ten times. The passage moves from God's character to Paul's experience (verses 8 to 11) and then to his conduct (verses 12 to 24). A play on “Yes” and “No” (verses 17 to 20) turns a defense of travel plans into a statement about the faithfulness of God. The final verse (verse 24) continues into 2:1-4, where Paul explains why he wrote rather than came.

outline.t: Changed plans and the Yes of God in Christ
Why Paul did not return: to spare them

doctrines.note: Suffering is shared: “the sufferings of Christ overflow to us” (verse 5), and so does comfort. Affliction taught Paul not to trust in himself but in God (verse 9), and the comfort he received equips him to comfort others. Suffering is neither denied nor explained away; it is given a purpose.
God is “the Father of compassion and the God of all comfort” (verse 3), faithful in his promises (verse 18), and the God “who raises the dead” (verse 9). The chapter's argument rests on who God is.
God has put “His Spirit in our hearts as a pledge of what is to come” (verse 22). The Spirit is the down payment of salvation, the present guarantee that God will finish what he has begun.
Paul depends on the Corinthians' prayers (verse 11) and expects that answered prayer will produce thanksgiving from many. Intercession draws the church into God's work of deliverance.

words.note: Paraklesis, comfort, encouragement, or exhortation, from a verb meaning to call alongside. It appears six times in verses 3 to 7 (and the verb four times). Biblical comfort is not sentimental soothing but strengthening presence, courage given to endure. The related word paraclete is used in John's Gospel for the Holy Spirit.

Thlipsis, affliction or trouble, literally pressure or crushing. Paul uses it for the hardships of his ministry and the sufferings of believers in general. In this chapter it is paired with comfort: God comforts in all affliction, not by removing it.

Arrabon, pledge, deposit, or down payment. A Semitic loanword used in Greek commerce for a first installment guaranteeing the full sum. The Spirit is God's arrabon (verse 22; also 5:5 and Ephesians 1:14), the first part of the life to come, given now as a guarantee.

Nai, yes. Paul's play on yes and no (verses 17 to 20) defends his reliability by pointing to Christ: “all the promises of God are ‘Yes’ in Christ.” Every promise God made to Israel finds its fulfillment and confirmation in Jesus.

christ: This chapter gives one of the great statements about Christ's relation to the Old Testament: “all the promises of God are ‘Yes’ in Christ” (verse 20). The promises to Abraham, to David, and through the prophets are confirmed and fulfilled in him, and the church's “Amen” to God is spoken through him. Christ's sufferings “overflow” to his people, and so does his comfort (verse 5), because believers share his life. The God “who raises the dead” (verse 9) is the God who raised Jesus, and the same power sustains Paul in despair. The Son of God preached among the Corinthians was never yes and no, but faithful, and he makes his people faithful too.

hard.q: If Paul was a faithful apostle, why did he despair even of life, and why did God let him come so close to death?
hard.a:
Paul does not hide the depth of his distress: he was “under a burden far beyond our ability to endure,” so that he “despaired even of life” (verse 8). The Bible does not present faithful people as immune to despair; the psalms of lament, Elijah under the broom tree, and Jesus in Gethsemane all show otherwise. Paul does not claim to know every reason for his suffering, but he names one purpose he saw in it: “in order that we would not trust in ourselves, but in God, who raises the dead” (verse 9). The experience stripped away his self-reliance and taught him to hope in resurrection power.

Some readers ask whether this contradicts promises of protection elsewhere. Paul's answer is that God's deliverance may come through suffering rather than instead of it, and ultimately through resurrection. He also says the ordeal served others, since the comfort he received became comfort he could give (verses 4 to 6). None of this makes suffering good in itself, but it shows that despair is not the end of faith.

Paul also did not carry his despair alone: he leaned on the prayers of others (verse 11) and on the comfort that came through other people (7:6). A reader who is near despair today should not carry it alone either. A pastor, a trusted friend, or a doctor can help, and anyone thinking of ending their life should contact a crisis line or emergency services right away (in the United States, call or text 988).

questions: Paul says God comforts us so that we can comfort others. When has someone comforted you in a way that came from their own suffering?
What would it mean for you to “not trust in ourselves, but in God, who raises the dead” in a situation you are facing now?
Paul's reliability was questioned. How do you respond when people misunderstand your motives or changed plans?
